3.5.title: Problemas
blocks: WHERE CAPACITY GETS LOST
Small Inefficiencies Become Expensive at Scale
Operational drag rarely comes from one dramatic failure. It builds through repeated manual steps, disconnected systems, unclear handoffs, and workarounds that no longer fit the business.
Your team copies data, prepares routine reports, routes requests, or sends the same follow-ups every day.
Important information lives across your CRM, inbox, accounting platform, forms, spreadsheets, and internal systems.
Re-keying data and relying on memory creates inconsistencies, missed steps, and avoidable rework.
More customers create more coordination, and hiring becomes the default answer to process problems.
Existing products solve most of the problem, but the remaining gap keeps forcing your team into manual workarounds.
You see potential, but need a grounded way to evaluate use cases, accuracy, risk, and expected value.
The goal is not to automate everything. It is to remove the right friction.

3.7.title: Principio de selección tecnológica
blocks: The Right Tool for the Work

Not every process needs AI. Predictable tasks often work best with straightforward rules and integrations. Messy, language-heavy work may benefit from AI. Unique operational gaps may require custom software. We choose based on reliability, cost, maintainability, and business value—not novelty.

AUTOMATION
Best for repeatable steps, clear rules, and consistent inputs.

AI
Best for interpreting, classifying, extracting, or drafting from unstructured information.

CUSTOM SOFTWARE
Best when your workflow is valuable, specific, and poorly served by existing products.
Often, the strongest solution combines all three.

3.9.title: Escenarios ilustrativos
blocks: EXAMPLE OUTCOMES
What Better Operations Could Look Like
The scenarios below are illustrative examples—not client case studies or guaranteed results. Estimates vary by workflow, volume, systems, and implementation quality.
Illustrative scenario
Faster Intake for a Professional Services Team
Requests arrive by email, staff re-enter details into a project system, create folders, assign owners, and send confirmation messages manually.
A structured intake flow extracts key details, validates required information, creates the record, routes the request, and flags exceptions for review.
At 180 requests per month and 12 minutes saved per request, the workflow could recover about 36 hours per month—before accounting for fewer corrections or faster response times.

~36 potential hours recovered / month
180 monthly requests
Human review for exceptions
Illustrative scenario
Connected Order Handoffs for a B2B Distributor
Sales details are copied from the CRM into operations and accounting systems, creating delays and mismatched records.
An integration validates required fields, creates downstream records, alerts the right owner, and logs sync failures for recovery.
At 320 orders per month and 8 minutes of duplicate entry avoided per order, the workflow could recover roughly 43 hours per month and reduce re-keying risk.

~43 potential hours recovered / month
320 monthly orders
Visible sync and exception log
Illustrative scenario
Quicker Document Review for an Operations Team
Staff open incoming documents, locate a standard set of fields, enter them into an internal tracker, and escalate incomplete submissions.
An AI-assisted workflow extracts and validates fields, highlights uncertainty, and requires a person to approve low-confidence or high-impact items.
At 500 documents per month and an average of 6 minutes saved per document, the workflow could recover about 50 hours per month while keeping review controls in place.

No. We use AI when the work requires interpretation of language or unstructured information and when the expected value justifies the added complexity. For predictable tasks, conventional automation is often simpler, more reliable, and less expensive.
